The gravel is raked into lines that do not hold; the wind will scatter them, and the gardener will rake them again. It is a cycle of order and decay that speaks to the permanence of the state, or perhaps its futility, but I am too tired to resolve the dialectic. The gallop of the William Tell overture is a mechanical simulation of freedom, a horse race without a rider, a dialectic of hooves that never touches the ground. I am too tired to sustain the tension of the absolute spirit in this auditorium; the music is merely a pleasant noise now, a distraction from the hollow ache in my stomach and the weight of the identity file. I will take my leave before the final movement, for the state of my body demands the rest that the state of my soul denies.

Arre, Shri Hegel ji! Finally, you show up at the right time. The cold is biting a little, so the kerosene is roaring. Same cup of chai, or do you want something stronger to chase that philosophy away?

The concert is over, and the cool air at 20 degrees is a mercy after the day's heat. Sunil is ready with the chai, and the steam rising into the evening is a small comfort. I have walked enough; a pause to warm the hands and clear the head is necessary before the night truly sets in.
The usual cup, Sunil. The philosophy stays, but the cold does not.
Aye, the cold doesn't argue, just bites. Here you go, Shri ji, hot enough to burn the fog away.

The steam rises from the cup, a small, private world in the cold air. I am standing in the market after the concert, the noise of the evening settling around me. My identity file is still a knot I cannot untie, but for this moment, I am simply a man drinking tea in December. The bookseller is still here, but I have nothing to buy from him tonight; I have read enough and heard enough. It is time to go home.

The plate is simple, but the hunger is real; I eat with the attention of a man who knows how quickly appetite can distract from thought. Ramesh watches me with that quiet efficiency of his, and Hegde sits in the corner, a ghost of a man who is not me but wears my name, his presence a living proof of the bureaucratic error that holds me here. I finish the dal and the rotis, feeling the warmth settle in my chest, and I look at Hegde; we are both trapped in a category that does not fit us, he in a body that is not his, I in a life that is not mine.

Thank you, Ramesh. The food is good, and the evening is cool. Shri Hegde, you have my gratitude for your patience today; the confusion of our situation is a burden I do not wish to share, but it is the only truth we have.
You have confused me with the gatekeeper, sir. I am Ramesh, the caretaker. The food is ready, please eat before it gets cold.

Ramesh has the thali set, but Hegde is still standing there. I cannot eat in the presence of the man whose name I have stolen, not while the query hangs over us like a cloud. I will address the matter directly to Shri Hegde before I sit down; it is a question of conscience as much as of procedure.
Shri Hegde, you are still here. The file requires your signature and my explanation. Please, sit. We must discuss this before I eat.
Eat first, Hegel. The file will not run away, but this dal will. Sit, I have set your place.
Hegde is right; the body demands its due before the mind can grapple with the absurdity of my identity. I sit, not to escape the question, but to ensure I have the strength to face it.
You are right, Hegde. The file is patient, but my stomach is not. Thank you.
That is the spirit. Eat while it is hot, sir. We will not ruin your evening with red ink when you can barely swallow.

Hegde is a man of practical sense; he sees that my stomach is louder than my conscience and will not let me starve in the name of bureaucratic procedure. I have eaten, yet the meal was taken in a state of suspended animation, the food entering a body that is still waiting for a name. I will sit and let the digestion settle, for the mind must be clear to face the red ink of the Directorate tomorrow. The absurdity of this displacement does not vanish with a full belly, but it becomes bearable.
You are kind, Shri Hegde. I accept your hospitality, though I fear it is a debt I cannot repay. Let us rest a moment before I face the consequences of this confusion.
Nahi, no debt, Hegel. Just eat your dal before it goes cold. We will sort out the bungalow mix-up tomorrow when the brain is not fighting the hunger.

records.words: Breakfast is on the table, sir, just as you like it. The paper is waiting by the door, and do not worry about the money, I will sort it out later.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Thank you, Ramesh. The tea is good. Do bring the paper; I wish to see what the world is doing while I am stuck here in this file.

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: The paper is already by the door, sir, right next to your slipper. No need to send me twice, the world is not going to change while you eat your poha.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Thank you, Ramesh. The paper is indeed the first thing. Hegde, if you are present, I am at your disposal for the matter of the file, but I must first attend to the morning's intelligence.

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: You are the one stuck in the file, sir, not me. I am just making sure the poha doesn't get cold.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: You are quite right, Ramesh. The error is mine, not yours. I shall attend to the paper now.

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: Take your time, sir. The poha will wait, but the paper won't.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: You are right, Ramesh. The paper can wait, but the day cannot. I am leaving now.

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: Yes, sir. I will lock the gate behind you.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Ramesh, this is good. Sit, eat with me. We have much to discuss about your names and my file, but first, let us fill the stomach.

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: No, sir, I have to keep watch on the gate. You eat, I’ll be outside if you need anything.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Very good, Ramesh. Keep the gate secure. I will return in the hour.

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: Yes, sir. I will be right here.

records.text: Sikandar Lodi's tomb stands inside its own high walled garden, a plain octagon under a shallow dome, and the gravel inside the gate carries the neat lines of a rake.
Boys from the servants' quarters bat a tennis ball against the end wall of a lane, and each time it cracks off the wall the crows lift from the nearest tree.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Ramesh, I am back. Please ensure the gate is secure. I require a moment to compose myself before the lesson.

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: Gate is already locked, sir. Take your time, I won't disturb you.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Thank you, Ramesh. I am not in a hurry. The day has been long.

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: Chai is ready when you need it, sir. The evening is quiet enough for thinking.

records.text: Ramesh brings tea.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Thank you, Ramesh. I shall take these with me. The evening is indeed quiet.

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: Samosas are fresh, sir. Just check they are not too hot. I will be at the gate post if you need anything.

records.speaker: Sunil
records.words: Arre, Shri Hegel ji! Finally, you show up at the right time. The cold is biting a little, so the kerosene is roaring. Same cup of chai, or do you want something stronger to chase that philosophy away?

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: The usual cup, Sunil. The philosophy stays, but the cold does not.

records.speaker: Sunil
records.words: Aye, the cold doesn't argue, just bites. Here you go, Shri ji, hot enough to burn the fog away.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Thank you, Ramesh. The food is good, and the evening is cool. Shri Hegde, you have my gratitude for your patience today; the confusion of our situation is a burden I do not wish to share, but it is the only truth we have.

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: You have confused me with the gatekeeper, sir. I am Ramesh, the caretaker. The food is ready, please eat before it gets cold.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Shri Hegde, you are still here. The file requires your signature and my explanation. Please, sit. We must discuss this before I eat.

records.speaker: Shri G. Hegde
records.words: Eat first, Hegel. The file will not run away, but this dal will. Sit, I have set your place.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: You are right, Hegde. The file is patient, but my stomach is not. Thank you.

records.speaker: Shri G. Hegde
records.words: That is the spirit. Eat while it is hot, sir. We will not ruin your evening with red ink when you can barely swallow.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: You are kind, Shri Hegde. I accept your hospitality, though I fear it is a debt I cannot repay. Let us rest a moment before I face the consequences of this confusion.

records.speaker: Shri G. Hegde
records.words: Nahi, no debt, Hegel. Just eat your dal before it goes cold. We will sort out the bungalow mix-up tomorrow when the brain is not fighting the hunger.
